thread.title: Netflix Has A New Competitor - YouTube - Netflix, NFLX)

author: Andri Capital
title: Netflix Has A New Competitor - YouTube - Netflix, NFLX)
text:
Hardly a day goes by that someone doesn’t mention Netflix (NASDAQ: NFLX ), or its main competitor Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN ) for that matter. But lurking in the shadows are a few smaller players that are ready to take on the big boys, one of which that is a force to be reckoned with: Alphabet's ( GOOG , GOOGL ) YouTube.
And here’s why:
YouTube Premium YouTube has not put a lot of effort into original content, until now. Last May 17, 2018 YouTube rebranded its previous YouTube Red service to YouTube Premium. YouTube Premium is basically a paid streaming subscription service for YouTube in the United States, Australia, Mexico, New Zealand, and South Korea, providing advertising-free streaming of all videos hosted by YouTube, exclusive original content and access to YouTube Music, similar to Apple Music ( AAPL ) or Spotify ( SPOT ).
The service originally focused on more native content, emphasizing programs by well-known YouTube personalities while keeping things close to the vest within YouTube’s own ecosystem and the already-built audiences of those specific personalities.
But now, as the service is becoming more fully developed and less experimental, it is venturing much more into the field of original content produced in collaboration with production studios - as the other streaming services (Netflix, Amazon, Hulu, etc.) have so successfully focused on. And YouTube has now given us a taste of what is to come, with the widely acclaimed and popular karate comedy series Cobra Kai .
Eyeballs, Brand, and Platform YouTube already has a very successful platform that is accessible online and through multiple media devices, TV's, etc. YouTube has over one billion users, reaching more 18-to-34- and 18-to-49-year-olds than any cable network in the US. It has launched local versions in more than 88 countries (although YouTube Premium is still limited to fewer countries). More than half of YouTube views come from mobile devices and in total the service generates billions of views each day.
YouTube also has a very recongnizable brand name and established record, being founded in 2005 and having operated for more than a decade in the online world.
So, although YouTube Premium may still not have as many registered subscribers yet, it does face lower barriers to entry into the streaming service market due to its already large audience of YouTube users.
Backed By Google YouTube is a subsidiary of Google (which again is a subsidiary of Alphabet) and therefore has a strong financial backing. The deep pockets of Google can thus enable YouTube to both develop the service, experiment with new ways, and most importantly produce content. That is, YouTube certainly has the capital required to support content creators and the production of high-quality original content to rival other streaming services.
Netflix's Moat Although Netflix has enjoyed a great success in recent years, its moat may not necessarily be as secure as one might think.
In general, subscribers go to where the most, best content is. And the most, best content gets produced where it is most likely to be seen (this is a “loop” that starts as the “chicken and egg” problem). Today, Netflix has a lot of great content which has attracted a strong subscriber base. And as long as Netflix can produce and provide the most, best content (or at least a very significant amount of such great content) it will retain its subscribers and sustain the earning power.
But the key competitive advantage therefore really lies in guaranteeing a large volume of high-quality content. This means supporting producers with capital and relevant services, enabling the creation of high-quality content. If the quality of the content was to start diminishing or the number of shows, movies or other entertainment to get smaller, or if competition heats up with alternatives offering more high-quality content, then the number of Netflix subscribers could fall.
So, today producers are likely most willing to go to Netflix (or Amazon) because that's were the viewers are. And Netflix has the capital to back them up - thereby keeping the "loop" going. But if an alternative service comes along with very many viewers then the competition may start to revolve around attracting the most, best content - providing producers with the best terms, support, services, etc. and most capital (basically, competing for content). And that's how Netflix's moat can start to shrink.
Conclusion As an investor in Netflix you would be smart to be concerned about competition in the streaming subscription service space. Although the space already has a few established players, such as Amazon and Hulu, it now has (or is about to have) a new power player that can stir things around.
YouTube, with the capital-backing of mighty Google, already has the viewers and thereby the potential subscribers (reachable with lower barriers to entry due to the already-established user base) to rival Netflix (and other streaming services).
It may be early days of YouTube Premium, but the release and success of the Cobra Kai series shows that YouTube can play in this space. Strong brand, widely used and easily accessible platform, and the capital to back it all up makes YouTube therefore a potentially fierce competitor. Also, having YouTube Music as a complementary to a YouTube Premium subscription is an added benefit that makes it even more attractive for prospective subscribers. The question then is really just whether they will start producing a significant enough volume of high-quality content to put a dent in Netflix’s moat.
